lines.trans: Hello, Viktoriya Sergeyevna.
What happened?
Viktoriya, we were robbed.
They stole a sauté pan.
And is that all?
You called me in over a saucepan?
I called you in for a reason.
Your Barinov stole the sauté pan.
We must stop him right now.
Otherwise tomorrow he will carry out the stove.
German, it is just a saucepan.
I might as well have called the police too.

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian interj meaning 'hi', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hi, I made an omelette for you.
Hello, Viktoriya Sergeyevna.

examples.text: Алло, Макс, привет, как вы там?
examples.trans: Hello, Max, hi, how are you doing there?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Well, and what does that mean?
What kind of nonsense is this?

examples.text: Не говори, что я забыл фрукты.
examples.trans: Do not say that I forgot the fruit.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (root 'лучиться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to happen', forming an aspectual pair with 'случаться'.

examples.trans: What happened?
What happened to me?
And what happened to the car?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('we') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: We are family, after all.
Soon we will have a baby.
We do not have any fruit.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (root 'ократь'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to robbed'.

examples.trans: We have been robbed!
Viktoriya, we were robbed.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (root 'красть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to steal', forming an aspectual pair with 'красть'.

examples.trans: They stole a sauté pan.
Your Barinov stole the sauté pan.
They stole a copper sauté pan.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'sauté', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Lyova, hand me the sauté pan.
I need my copper sauté pan.
Your copper sauté pan stayed there.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And is that all?
And your sauté pan is fine.

examples.text: И майка у него с пауком.
examples.trans: And he has a shirt with a spider.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Но хуже всего, когда вас игнорируют.
examples.trans: But worst of all is when they ignore you.
I understood everything, chef.
Come on, everything is fine.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: It is always nice when people love you.

examples.text: Но хуже всего, когда вас игнорируют.
examples.trans: But worst of all is when they ignore you.
You have a day off today, right?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Hi, I made an omelette for you.
Have you forgiven me?
I slept so well.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (root 'звать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to call', forming an aspectual pair with 'вызывать'.

examples.trans: You called me in over a saucepan?

examples.text: Я вызвал вас не просто так.
examples.trans: I called you in for a reason.
I might as well have called the police too.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'because of' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We quarrel over such little things.
You called me in over a saucepan?

examples.text: Из-за этой ерунды вы нас вызвали?
examples.trans: You called us in over this nonsense?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'pot', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: You called me in over a saucepan?
German, it is just a saucepan.
Who touched my favorite pot?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('not') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Не стоит злиться друг на друга.
examples.trans: There is no point getting angry at each other.
Do not give him too much, okay?
Do not tell Nastya.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.

examples.text: Я вызвал вас не просто так.
examples.trans: I called you in for a reason.
German, it is just a saucepan.
I simply slipped.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I slept so well.

examples.text: Я вызвал вас не просто так.
examples.trans: I called you in for a reason.
Here is the plan, we have to steal the safe.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: Your copper sauté pan stayed there.
Your Barinov stole the sauté pan.

examples.text: На вашем месте я бы не спорил.
examples.trans: In your place, I would not argue.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('he') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: It was in the other restaurant.
I need it right now.
He is climbing into the oven right now!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'necessary'.

examples.trans: I need to make a call.
You need to rest.

examples.text: Мне нужно позвонить губернатору. Дай телефон.
examples.trans: I need to call the governor. Give me a phone.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.trans: I need it right now.
Yes, I will be right there.
He is climbing into the oven right now!

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to stop', forming an aspectual pair with 'останавливать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: We must stop him right now.
A dubious way to stop me.
Stop the car!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Well, and what does that mean?
Otherwise it will go badly.
And I will say that I brought them.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'otherwise', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: We were starting to worry, you see.
Faster, or we'll be late.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'tomorrow'.

examples.text: А то завтра он вынесет плиту.
examples.trans: Otherwise tomorrow he will carry out the stove.
We'll arrange something for tomorrow.
See you tomorrow!

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (root 'нести'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'issue', forming an aspectual pair with 'выносить'.

examples.text: А то завтра он вынесет плиту.
examples.trans: Otherwise tomorrow he will carry out the stove.
Carrying it out unnoticed will not work.
The judge handed down a strict decision.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'stove', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: А то завтра он вынесет плиту.
examples.trans: Otherwise tomorrow he will carry out the stove.

examples.text: Внимательно смотри за температурой на плите.
examples.trans: Watch carefully the temperature on the stove.

examples.text: Я сниму сковороду с горячей плиты вовремя.
examples.trans: I will remove the pan from the hot stove on time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('this') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Well, and what does that mean?
What kind of nonsense is this?
That was not me, that was Styopa.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('but') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We are family, after all.
You have a day off today, right?
Children bring people closer, right?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('would') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I might as well have called the police too.

examples.text: А если бы у вас украли пистолет?
examples.trans: And what if someone stole a pistol from you?

examples.text: На вашем месте я бы не спорил.
examples.trans: In your place, I would not argue.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'more'.

examples.trans: I still need to unpack my things.
I might as well have called the police too.
Maybe we should play the cities game too?

meanings.note: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German 'Polizei' / French 'police' (from Greek 'politeia', civil administration).

examples.trans: I might as well have called the police too.

examples.text: Вам не нужны проблемы с полицией.
examples.trans: You do not need problems with the police.
Now let the police sort it out.
